periods.label: On Human Nature

levels.sentence: In my journal I set down these sharp, candid observations on human nature—vanity, self-deception, flattery, and the little tricks by which we fool ourselves and one another.
levels.paragraph: In my journal I set down these observations because human nature is a spectacle that never ceases to amuse me. A sick man may grow fat on his disease once his mind gives over struggling; a self-conceited fellow remembers the clever talk that his mother ought to have whipped out of him; and a man who is perpetually flattered may wonder he is not already a cinder. I have remarked that a tailor chooses an absurd colour precisely to draw every eye, that women may spin but cannot compose a good cookery book, and that when I bought a flageolet I never once made out a tune. There is a change of modes in the whole department of life, but the little perversities of human kind remain constant.
levels.summary:
I have been turning over my notes on human nature, and the follies I find are endless. A man whose mind has ceased to struggle with disease grows fat upon it; another, perpetually flattered in every mode, should long ago have been blown into a cinder by so many bellows.

I remember the self-conceited stuff I once talked to my mother, and she ought to have whipped me for it. —and in gambling, superior skill is no roguery, for the loser honestly thinks he can play better.

Where judgement is concerned, I speak plainly. Foote is impartial, for he tells lies of everybody; Burke is an extraordinary man, with a perpetual stream of mind.

A lady who sets herself up for ridicule is like a chimney already black—you cannot blacken it further—and I said of one lady that she was very fit for a brothel.

We may admire a fine fiddler yet like him as little as a toad, and in proportion to his size a good bull-dog has strength, or your argument would make a small one as weak as a mouse. As for gossip, they are always telling lies of us old fellows.

As for old age, I have no wish to know its evils beforehand: would you have the gout, would you have decrepitude? Yet I am not uneasy at the thought of dying, for I shall keep my consciousness and carry all my goods with me.

The little particulars of life betray us all. A tailor chooses a strange colour because it will draw crowds to see how well he can make a coat even of so absurd a colour; women can spin, but they cannot make a good book of cookery; and I confess I once bought a flageolet but never made out a tune.

Modes change—great families no longer keep state servants—but the same excuses and superstitions remain. Old Mr. Sheridan has found a very good reason, and for my part I think a poker set upright across the grate is better than the old trick for driving away a witch.

I act from both motive and instinct when I shoot a highwayman; a man who would be driven from the stage by a line might be driven from his shop by another; and there were no more six horses than six phoenixes.

periods.label: On Happiness

levels.sentence: By attending to little things, we gain the art of minimizing misery and maximizing happiness, yet happiness itself comes in degrees, depending on one's capacity for agreeable consciousness.
levels.paragraph: I have learned that nothing is too little for so small a creature as man. It is by studying little things that we attain the great art of having as little misery and as much happiness as possible. I also see that happiness is not equal for all; a peasant and a philosopher may be equally satisfied but not equally happy. Happiness consists in the multiplicity of agreeable consciousness, and a peasant lacks the capacity for the same degree of happiness as a philosopher.
levels.summary:
I have come to see that the secret to a contented life lies in paying attention to little things, for nothing is too small for so little a creature as man. By studying these small matters, we can master the great art of reducing misery and increasing happiness, making the most of our limited existence.

Yet I also recognize that happiness is not a single uniform state. While a peasant and a philosopher may both feel satisfied, their happiness differs in degree.

True happiness depends on the multiplicity of agreeable consciousness—the range and richness of awareness—and a peasant, lacking that capacity, cannot experience the same height of happiness as a philosopher.

periods.label: On Politics

levels.sentence: I love the University of Salamanca for ruling that the Spanish conquest of America was unlawful, I would drive every rascal from my county if I owned a great estate, and I knocked Fox on the head while warning Reynolds that he is always under some star or constellation.
levels.paragraph: I have been reflecting on judgment and influence. I love the University of Salamanca because, when the Spaniards doubted the lawfulness of conquering America, it bravely said that it was not lawful. In electioneering, I confessed that if I were a man of great estate I would drive out all the rascals I disliked from the county. And I told Reynolds that I knocked Fox on the head without ceremony, and that he is too much under Fox and Burke — always under some planet.
levels.summary:
Today I praised the University of Salamanca, for when the Spaniards were in doubt about the lawfulness of conquering America, that learned body gave its opinion that it was not lawful. I love them for that honest judgment.

Later, speaking of elections, I admitted that if I were a man of great estate I would drive all the rascals I did not like out of the county at an election.

I also boasted that I knocked Fox on the head without ceremony, and I warned Reynolds that he is too much under Fox and Burke at present. He is under the Fox star and the Irish constellation — he is always under some planet.

My point is that a man should not let himself be swayed by others, no matter how bright their stars appear.

periods.label: On Education & Learning

levels.sentence: Dr Johnson, pointing at me, declared that I had been idle in Edinburgh, Glasgow, and London and would be idle in Utrecht, and then in conversation he argued that even great lawyers know other subjects, that education after twenty-five is too late, and that lawyers possess practical knowledge of life which bookish men need.
levels.paragraph: I felt the heat rise as Johnson pointed at me and announced to the company that I had been idle everywhere—Edinburgh, Glasgow, London, and soon Utrecht. When I asked him privately how he could expose me so, he answered with his usual bluntness. He went on to defend lawyers, citing Hale and Selden as men who wrote on law but knew many other things, and insisted that a person should not try to begin serious learning after twenty-five. Most of all, he valued lawyers for their practical knowledge of life, saying that a bookish man should always have them to converse with.
levels.summary:
Johnson teased me publicly by tracing my idleness from Edinburgh to Glasgow to London and prophesying the same at Utrecht, and I privately asked how he could expose me so.

He then turned to a defense of lawyers, pointing out that Judge Hale and Selden were great lawyers who nonetheless wrote on many other subjects, showing that law need not narrow a mind.

On the subject of age and learning, he said he would have thought differently if he had been sent to college from fifteen to twenty-five, but not from twenty-five to thirty-five, implying that the proper season for education is early youth.

Finally, he called lawyers practical men of the world whose knowledge of life is exactly what a bookish man lacks, and advised that a studious person should always have them to converse with.

periods.label: On Places & Travel

levels.sentence: In my journal I recorded Dr. Johnson's laughing tease that Scotland is all gardening and that London contains all life can afford, along with his quick sayings on mapping and driving.
levels.paragraph: In my journal I set down Dr. Johnson's teasing paradoxes: he said Scotland is all gardening, that a country must be travelled over to be mapped, that driving is always from or to something, and that Scots have enough meat and drink only to run away from home. Yet when he spoke of London, his voice grew warm, for he declared that every intellectual man is unwilling to leave it, and that to be tired of London is to be tired of life. I felt both stung and delighted by his wit, knowing his affection lay with the great city rather than my northern home.
levels.summary:
Dr. Johnson came to see me, and in the middle of our talk he leaned back in his chair and laughed, teasing me about Scottish gardening. He insisted that with us everything needs cultivation, even the sloe, which grows wild in England.

I felt the familiar flush of national pride mixed with amusement at his grand exaggerations.

He then tossed off aphorisms as if they were coins: a country must be travelled over before it can be mapped; driving is always from something or to something; and Scotland gives its inhabitants just enough meat and drink to run away from home.

I recorded each saying in this journal, struck by how neatly he turned our poverty into a joke.

Finally he praised London with a seriousness I had not expected. No man of any intellect willingly leaves it, he said; to be tired of London is to be tired of life, for it contains all that life can afford.

I left our conversation feeling the pull of two places—my wild, cultivated Scotland and his all-sufficient London.

periods.label: On Books & Writing

levels.sentence: In my journal I recorded Dr. Johnson's scattered pronouncements on books and writing—from comedy and farce to cadence, sales, and the limits of description.
levels.paragraph: In these jottings I preserved Johnson's talk about literature. He distinguished comedy from farce, praised Temple for giving prose cadence, and doubted his own judgement about book sales. He admitted he had dedicated to the whole Royal family, though only the last generation. He also quoted Gravina to explain why description excites curiosity but seeing satisfies it.
levels.summary:
At my table with Dr. Johnson, I noted down his remarks on books and writing. He said of Shakespeare's editors that to name one would force him to name many—Mrs. Pritchard, Mrs. Cibber, and even Mr. Cibber, who also altered Shakespeare.

When we talked of comedy, he insisted that true comedy exhibits a species, like a miser gathered from many misers, while farce only exhibits individuals; he called farce a vice, not a talent.

Johnson also spoke of prose cadence, crediting Sir William Temple with first giving it to English; before him writers were careless how sentences ended. He owned that his judgement was no certain rule for a book's sale, and that his Journey to the Hebrides had not sold greatly.

On travel writing he quoted Gravina: every man desires to see what he has read, but none desires to read an account of what he has seen; description only excites curiosity, seeing satisfies it. He teased me about Pennant's Alnwick, saying Pennant had done what he intended by making me very angry.

periods.label: On Religion

levels.sentence: Religious truth is established only through the mutual witness of persecution and patient endurance, and most of what we believe, in religion as in life, rests on implicit faith.
levels.paragraph: I told Sir that the Presbyterians have no church and no apostolical ordination, for their claim to religious truth lacks the ancient seal. On martyrdom, I insisted that the magistrate has a right to enforce what he thinks, while the man who is conscious of the truth has a right to suffer; there is no other way to ascertain truth than by persecution on one side and endurance on the other. When a lady asked about implicit faith, I answered that the greatest part of our knowledge is implicit faith, and asked whether we have heard all that a disciple of Confucius or a Mahometan can say for himself. In all this, I held that religious certainty comes not from comfortable inquiry but from standing firm under trial and trusting what we have received.
levels.summary:
I told Sir plainly that the Presbyterians have no church, no apostolical ordination — their separation cuts them off from the succession Christ ordained.

When we spoke of martyrdom, I said that the only way religious truth is established is by martyrdom: the magistrate may enforce what he thinks, and he who is certain of the truth may suffer for it.

I confessed I am afraid there is no other method of ascertaining truth than persecution on the one hand and endurance on the other. Persecution is the price of certainty, and suffering is the seal of conviction.

Afterwards, when Madam questioned me about implicit faith, I told her that most of our knowledge is implicit faith. We have not heard all that a disciple of Confucius or a Mahometan can say for himself, yet we hold our religion true; so even in religion we lean on testimony we cannot fully examine.

I felt that honest inquiry leads us to acknowledge how much we take on faith, and that the truest faith is proved not by argument alone but by willingness to suffer.

periods.label: On Conversation

levels.sentence: In the art of conversation, one must avoid self-love and repetition, curb curiosity, and acknowledge the two motives of speech—benevolence or selfishness—while noting that young men inhibit real exchange and that even Burke's serious excellence collapses when he attempts humor.
levels.paragraph: In my reflections on conversation, I have noted many pitfalls: self-love makes a man dislike hearing himself, repetition bores, and curiosity must be curbed. Young men stifle real exchange because men of character refuse to stake their reputation before them. Politeness often requires a courteous denial, and counting by twos only prolongs folly. I have also observed that speech is driven either by benevolence to instruct or by selfishness for distinction. Even the great Burke, superior in serious talk, descends to the kennel when he tries to be merry.
levels.summary:
In my reflections, I have observed that conversation is a delicate art. Self-love makes a man dislike his own praise, repetition brings him back to his starting point, and curiosity must be withheld from satisfaction.

Young men, moreover, inhibit true discourse, for a man of character will not risk his reputation before them. Politeness often requires a courteous denial, and counting by twos only prolongs the exchange unnecessarily.

Contempt is universally resented, so one must never treat another with it, yet approval should be given when due. I have also discerned that speech springs from two motives: the benevolent desire to instruct or entertain, and the selfish pursuit of distinction.

Even the celebrated Burke, whose serious conversation is superior beyond proportion, loses all measure when he descends to jest, becoming like one in the kennel.

periods.label: On Friendship

levels.sentence: After returning to Scotland, I wrote three letters to Johnson and then on the 2nd of May asked for another meeting in the North of England that autumn, while Langton sent word about Beauclerk and Johnson, and I recorded Johnson's remark that a friend had perhaps got there sooner through intimacy with him.
levels.paragraph: After my return to Scotland, I kept our friendship alive by writing three letters to him. On the 2nd of May I wrote again, requesting a meeting somewhere in the North of England in the autumn. Soon after, Mr. Langton sent me a letter with a passage about Mr. Beauclerk and Dr. Johnson. I recalled Johnson's remark that a friend had perhaps got to it sooner through intimacy with him, a sign of the influence such closeness could have.
levels.summary:
After returning to Scotland, I wrote three letters to Johnson, determined to keep our friendship strong across the distance. On the 2nd of May I wrote once more, proposing that we meet in the North of England that autumn. From Mr. Langton I soon received a letter containing a passage that touched on both Mr.

Beauclerk and Dr. Johnson, and I extracted it as a record of our circle.

This exchange was part of a larger thread of friendship built on intimacy and correspondence. Johnson had once said that a friend had perhaps got to something sooner through intimacy with him—a remark that stayed with me as proof of the influence such closeness could have on a person.

The letters, the planned meeting, and Langton's news all reminded me how friendship continues through shared attention and care.

periods.label: On Marriage

levels.sentence: I maintain that marriages would generally be as happy, and often more so, if arranged by the Lord Chancellor upon due consideration of characters and circumstances, without the parties having any choice.
levels.paragraph: In my observations on marriage, I have noted that forgetfulness is relative: a wife has many things she may think of, while a husband has many things he must think of. Regarding low birth, I remarked that a man might wash his bride's face and dress her cleanly, and if she had a bottom of good sense, she did not disgrace him. Ultimately, I believe that marriages would in general be as happy, and often more so, if they were all made by the Lord Chancellor, upon a due consideration of characters and circumstances, without the parties having any choice in the matter.
levels.summary:
During our conversations on marriage, I observed that forgetfulness depends on one's obligations. Mrs. Thrale, having many things she may think of, will forget first, while her husband, with many things he must think of, is less likely to forget.

I also spoke of a woman of low birth, noting that if her husband washed her face and put clean clothes on her, she did not disgrace him because she possessed a bottom of good sense.

I further declared my belief that marriages would generally be as happy, and often more so, if they were all made by the Lord Chancellor, upon a due consideration of characters and circumstances, without the parties having any choice.

This reflects my conviction that reason and prudence should govern the most important decision of life, rather than mere inclination.

periods.label: On Drink

levels.sentence: Wine does not produce light, gay hilarity but noisy, clamorous merriment—so do not feel obliged to drink with company, since there is no more reason for your drinking with him than for his being sober with you.
levels.paragraph: I argued that wine excites not light and gay ideal hilarity but a tumultuous, noisy, clamorous merriment; indeed, I have heard none of those drunken—no, drunken is too coarse—vinous flights. Then I reflected that it would be sad if we were obliged to drink or do anything agreeable to the company. Finally, I contended that there is no more reason for your drinking with him than for his being sober with you.
levels.summary:
I spoke of wine's true effect: it does not give light, gay, ideal hilarity, but rather a tumultuous, noisy, clamorous merriment. I have heard none of those drunken—drunken is a coarse word—none of those vinous flights.

I then considered social pressure: what a sad thing it would be if we were obliged to drink, or to do anything else that might happen to be agreeable to the company where we are. And on the matter of drinking with a companion, I said there is no more reason for your drinking with him than for his being sober with you.

periods.label: On Money

levels.sentence: Wealth alone proves no excellence, commercial life mixes cheating with kindness, an orchard is affordable if you rent the ground, and domestic spending brings the truest satisfaction.
levels.paragraph: I have often observed that a hundred thousand pounds is no proof of excellence, for a scoundrel commissary can amass it. In commercial dealings, I find people cheat more than I expected, yet they also show more kindness to one another. As for orchards, it is foolish to avoid having one merely to prove you cannot; for forty shillings rent you can grow trees, and graze beneath them once they mature. And I maintain that no money is better spent than on domestic satisfaction — a man delights that his wife is dressed as well as others, and she delights in being dressed.
levels.summary:
I have learned that wealth is no test of excellence, for I have seen a scoundrel commissary gain a hundred thousand pounds. In my commercial dealings, I found more cheating than I had imagined, yet also more mutual goodwill than I ever conceived possible.

On practical matters, I advise that one should not try to have a thing merely to prove one cannot have it; an orchard from rented ground costs little, and once the trees are grown, the same ground can be grazed.

And I hold that money spent on domestic satisfaction is the best spent of all, for it pleases both a man and his wife — he that she is dressed as well as others, and she that she is dressed.

levels.paragraph: I spent 1760 collecting these small wonders and contradictions. I noticed a man whose mind had stopped struggling with his illness, and he grew fat on it; I even mentioned my dedications to the Royal family all round, meaning the last generation. In conversation with Sir I insisted that a good bulldog may be as small as a mouse if his strength matches his size, and I answered his point about a line driving a man from the stage by saying another line would have driven him from his shop. I had to confess I once bought a flageolet and never made out a tune, and I warned that if you count by twos you may be long enough.
levels.summary:
At the opening of 1760 I found myself watching a man whose mind had given up the fight against his disease, so he simply grew fat upon it—a strange surrender that stuck with me.

I also recalled that I had dedicated my writings to the Royal family all round, at least to the last generation of them, as if casting my net wide but not too wide.

Across the year my talk with Sir kept returning to the power of proportions. I argued that strength comes in proportion to size, so a good bulldog might as well be as small as a mouse.

When he claimed a single line could drive a man from the stage, I answered that another line would have driven him from his shop: the same weapon has different reach.

I admitted I once bought a flageolet but never produced a tune from it, and I ended one exchange by warning that counting by twos could go on long enough.

levels.sentence: In 1763 I recorded Dr. Johnson's wisdom that man must study little things to lessen misery and increase happiness, and I felt the sting of his public rebuke when he called me idle, yet his teasing reply and his strange tales taught me to laugh at myself.
levels.paragraph: In 1763 I noted Johnson's maxim that there is nothing too little for so little a creature as man, and that by studying little things we attain the great art of having as little misery and as much happiness as possible. But that same day he pointed at me before a lady and said I had been idle at Edinburgh, Glasgow, London, and would be idle in Utrecht. I asked him privately how he could expose me so, and he answered that it was the sort of stuff he used to talk to his mother when he first thought himself clever, and that she ought to have whipt me. He then laughed on to other matters—a tailor who made a coat of an absurd colour to draw crowds, and a man so flattered by every bellows that he should have become a cinder. Old Mr. Sheridan, he added, had found out a very good reason, though I did not press for it.
levels.summary:
In 1763 I filled my journal with Dr. Johnson's sayings, beginning with his gentle maxim that man, being a little creature, must study little things to gain the great art of having as little misery and as much happiness as possible.

Then, in company, he pointed at me and told a lady that I had been idle at Edinburgh, sent to Glasgow where I continued idle, came to London where I was very idle, and was now going to Utrecht to be as idle as ever. I felt the hot sting of public exposure and asked him privately how he could shame me so.

He only laughed and said that was the sort of stuff he used to talk to his mother when he first thought himself clever, and that she ought to have whipt him.

From that same conversation I recorded his other observations: that a tailor had made a coat of a strange colour on purpose, knowing the absurd colour would draw crowds to see him and admire his skill even in such a coat; and that a man who is perpetually flattered by every conceivable mode has so many bellows blowing the fire that one wonders he is not by this time become a cinder.

He added that old Mr. Sheridan had found out a very good reason, though I leave that thread hanging. What stays with me is my own embarrassment and his unsparing wit—he turned my idleness into a joke and taught me again to value little things.

levels.sentence: In 1765 I delivered a handful of characteristic remarks, touching on Shakespeare's adapters, a friend's advantage through intimacy with me, and my refusal to disclose certain fates.
levels.paragraph: In 1765, in conversation, I made several points with my usual roundness. When a gentleman suggested I had omitted someone from mention, I replied that had I mentioned him, I must have named many more, including Mrs. Pritchard, Mrs. Cibber, and even Mr. Cibber, who likewise altered Shakespeare. I told another that a man perhaps reached his goal sooner because of his intimacy with me. To a question about someone's fate, I answered, "Nay, Sir, you shall know their fate no further," and to a lady I confessed I could not recollect the time she spoke of.
levels.summary:
These are four of my sayings from 1765, the year my edition of Shakespeare was published. In the first, I defended an omission by observing that if I named one adapter of Shakespeare, I would have to name a crowd—Mrs. Pritchard, Mrs. Cibber, and Mr. Cibber among them.

The remark shows my impatience with the long line of stage-folk who had manhandled the Bard.

Elsewhere I noted that a certain man had perhaps arrived at his success sooner through intimacy with me, a quiet boast in the guise of a casual aside.

To Sir I refused to disclose what had become of some people—"Nay, Sir, you shall know their fate no further"—and when a lady suggested a time when something was the case, I could only say I did not recollect it. The tone throughout is the tone of a man who enjoys holding the room with epigrams and reservations.

levels.sentence: In 1770 I held forth on marriage, money, wine, and language, letting no folly pass uncorrected.
levels.paragraph: This year my talk ran in every direction: I defended a woman from ridicule, told a lawyer he was worth more to me than books, and broke with superstition by setting a poker upright. I gave Boswell and the ladies plenty to repeat, though I would not be bound by every jest. The tone was brisk, sometimes cruel, but always aimed at truth.
levels.summary:
I passed 1770 in talk, as usual, with Boswell setting down my words. I told him why young men spoil conversation, why lawyers are the best companions for a bookish man, and why no one should be forced to drink merely to please the company.

I also made it plain that getting a hundred thousand pounds proves nothing, and that wine gives clamorous merriment, not gay hilarity.

On women and marriage I was not always gentle. I said one lady was fit for a brothel, yet I defended another against ridicule and praised a woman of good sense. I argued that a wife's dress is money well spent, and that marriages might be happier if the Lord Chancellor chose the partners.

I took care to correct false ideas about language, reminding people that English need not copy foreign words and that Sir William Temple first gave cadence to our prose.

I mocked superstition with a poker, advised a man not to rent an orchard just to prove he could not have it, and asked whether anyone truly wished to feel the evils of old age. Through all this I kept my own counsel: a man carries all he owns within him.

levels.paragraph: In 1772 I set down Johnson's opinions on roguery at the card table and his boast of knocking Fox on the head. He said Reynolds was always under some planet, now Fox, now Burke. On May 2 I wrote to Johnson proposing an autumn meeting in the North of England. Soon after, Langton sent me a letter with a passage about Beauclerk and Johnson.
levels.summary:
In 1772 I was at work recording Johnson's table-talk. He argued that it was no roguery for a master of a game to win money from a man who thought he could play better; superior skill carried it.

He also told me, with a laugh, that he had knocked Fox on the head without ceremony, and warned that Reynolds was always under some planet—now under Fox and Burke, now under some other influence. These sayings show his combative wit and his amused eye on his friends' political stars.

Meanwhile I was trying to arrange the pleasures of the next autumn. On the 2nd of May I wrote to Johnson himself, asking that we might meet again somewhere in the North of England. About the same time a letter came from Langton, and from it I extracted a passage that touched on both Beauclerk and Johnson.

I felt the warmth and complexity of our circle—rivalry, affection, and the constant hum of letters passing between us.

levels.sentence: In 1773 I filled my journal with Dr. Johnson's sayings and my own thoughts, from the lawfulness of the Spanish conquest to the perpetual stream of Burke's mind, as we journeyed through Scotland and the Hebrides.
levels.paragraph: In the year 1773, I wrote down the many conversations I had with Dr. Johnson during our tour of the Hebrides and after our return to Scotland. He spoke with authority on a wide array of topics: he cited the University of Salamanca's opinion against the conquest of America, mocked the Scottish attempts to cultivate the sloe, and argued that religious truth is established through persecution and endurance. I also reflected on my own correspondence with him and on the extraordinary powers of Burke, whose stream of mind is perpetual. This journal captures the wit and wisdom of a remarkable year.
levels.summary:
During my tour of the Hebrides with Dr. Johnson in 1773, I recorded his observations on a variety of subjects.

He spoke of the University of Salamanca's opinion that conquering America was unlawful, and he contrasted English and Scottish gardening, jesting about whether the Scots could ever bring the sloe to perfection.

He also discussed the lack of a church among Presbyterians, the role of martyrdom in establishing religious truth, and the importance of traveling over a country to map it.

After our return to Scotland, I wrote three letters to him, and I continued to reflect on the brilliance of Burke, whose conversation was like a perpetual stream.

' I also pondered the nature of description versus seeing, as Johnson quoted the Italian critic Gravina, and I considered the changes in modes across society, from household servants to the very purpose of motion.

Throughout the journal, I captured the essence of Johnson's mind: his firm opinions on religion, law, and manners, his wit in mocking Scottish gardening, and his philosophical insights into truth and reality.

The record of this year is a treasure of Enlightenment thought, seen through the lens of my deep admiration for my friend and companion.

Throughout the journal, I captured the essence of Johnson's mind: his firm opinions on religion, law, and manners, his wit in mocking Scottish gardening, and his philosophical insights into truth and reality.

The record of this year is a treasure of Enlightenment thought, seen through the lens of my deep admiration for my friend and companion.

levels.sentence: In the 1760s I filled my journal with Dr. Johnson's unsparing wit and my own epigrams, but the thread binding it all is my acknowledged idleness and the small, careful studies I was continually taught to value.
levels.paragraph: In 1760 I was drawn to a man who had surrendered to his disease and grown fat on it, and I thought again of my dedications to the last generation of the Royal family. My talks with Sir kept circling back to proportions: strength is relative to size, so a good bulldog might as well be a mouse, and while Johnson could drive a man from the stage with one line, I could drive him from his shop with another. In 1763 Johnson publicly mocked my idleness before a lady, and though I felt the sting, I treasured his wisdom that a little creature must study little things to have as little misery and as much happiness as possible. I set down his images of the tailor and the flattered cinder, my own definitions of vice and farce, and in 1765 I defended my Shakespeare by refusing to name the crowd of adapters. The whole decade, I see, was a practice in turning embarrassment into epigram.
levels.summary:
In 1760 I found myself watching a man whose mind had yielded to disease and grown fat upon it, and I recalled my dedications to the last generation of the Royal family. My conversations with Sir returned again and again to proportions: strength belongs to size, so a good bulldog might as well be as small as a mouse.

When Johnson claimed a single line could drive a man from the stage, I answered that another line would drive him from his shop. I confessed I had bought a flageolet but never produced a tune, and I warned that counting by twos could go on long enough.

In 1763 I filled my journal with Dr. Johnson's sayings, beginning with his gentle maxim that little man must study little things to gain the great art of having as little misery and as much happiness as possible.

Then, in company, he pointed at me and told a lady I had been idle at Edinburgh, sent to Glasgow where I continued idle, came to London where I was very idle, and was going to Utrecht to be as idle as ever.

I felt the hot sting of public exposure and asked him privately how he could shame me; he only laughed and said it was the sort of stuff he used to talk to his mother, and she ought to have whipt him.

I also recorded his image of the tailor who made an absurd-coloured coat on purpose to draw crowds, and of the flattered man with so many bellows blowing the fire that he should be a cinder. He added that old Mr. Sheridan had found out a very good reason, though I left that thread hanging.

By 1764 I had my own epigram: not a talent but a vice, not comedy but farce.

In 1765, the year my Shakespeare edition was published, I defended my omissions by saying I would have to name a crowd of adapters—Mrs. Pritchard, Mrs. Cibber, and Mr. Cibber among them. I also let slip that a certain man's success had perhaps come sooner through intimacy with me, a quiet boast.

To Sir I refused to disclose some people's fate: "Nay, Sir, you shall know their fate no further," and to a lady I said I did not recollect.

levels.sentence: In the 1770s, I recorded Dr. Johnson's table-talk, capturing his witty sayings, his firm opinions, and his occasional admissions of uncertainty.
levels.paragraph: During that decade, I spent many hours in Johnson's company, noting down his every remark. He discoursed on lawyers and love, on money and happiness, and on the superiority of London. Our tour of the Hebrides in 1773 gave me a treasure of his observations, and I came to admire his mind even when his judgments were harsh. Through my journal, I preserved the voice of a man who was, to me, the greatest of his age.
levels.summary:
Throughout the 1770s, I kept a detailed record of Dr. Johnson's conversation. He spoke on why lawyers make the best companions for a bookish man, why money proves nothing, and why wine only brings clamorous merriment.

I also noted his forthright views on women and marriage—he criticized one lady harshly, defended another, and even suggested the Lord Chancellor choose marriage partners. He corrected common errors about language and mocked superstition, always insisting that a man carries all he owns within himself.

Our friendship deepened over the decade. In 1772, I wrote to him about meeting in the North, and in 1773 we journeyed to the Hebrides together. There I recorded his thoughts on religion, on the differences between English and Scottish gardening, and on the nature of truth.

He praised Burke's conversation as a perpetual stream and quoted Gravina on description versus seeing. Our circle—Langton, Beauclerk, Reynolds, and others—was marked by warmth and rivalry, with letters constantly passing among us.

Johnson's table-talk from these years remains vivid to me: his distinction in 1776 between satisfaction and happiness, his declaration in 1777 that a man tired of London is tired of life, and his honest admission in 1775 that his judgment was no certain rule for a book's sale.

He could be combative, but he was also willing to admit uncertainty. These records are my attempt to capture the brilliance and complexity of a man I deeply admired.

In my journal I set down reflections on human nature, happiness, politics, religion, conversation, friendship, marriage, drink, and money — always preserving Johnson's voice and my own rejoinders.

periods.paragraph: I spent decades recording the talk of Dr. Johnson and my own musings, finding that even public mockery could be refined into wit. From his scolding about my idleness to his paradoxes about Scotland and London, I hoarded his wisdom. The little perversities of humankind, I concluded, remain constant even as modes change. What I learned above all was to study little things, for nothing is too little for so small a creature as man.
